en: Fermenting bagoong uses lactic acid bacteria to lower pH, preventing harmful bacterial growth and keeping the traditional shrimp paste safe to eat.
The flexible bamboo structure of a traditional bahay kubo absorbs seismic waves, making it safer during earthquakes than rigid concrete houses.
Wearing a mask during dusty Ati-Atihan festival dances prevents inhaling ash and soot, protecting your lungs from severe respiratory irritation.
Emptying stagnant water around your home eliminates breeding sites for Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, fulfilling your civic duty to prevent dengue outbreaks.
Ifugao stone-walling in rice terraces prevents soil erosion and landslides during heavy rains, ensuring safe and stable farmland for the community.
The Department of Health scientifically approves lagundi leaves as an effective herbal medicine for relieving coughs by acting as a natural bronchodilator.
The San Fernando Giant Lantern Festival uses LED lights instead of traditional bulbs to prevent electrical overheating and reduce pavilion fire risks.
Philippine revolutionaries used boiled guava leaves as a natural antiseptic to clean wounds and prevent deadly bacterial infections during the independence war.
The Philippine Clean Air Act mandates phasing out chlorofluorocarbons in old refrigerators to protect the ozone layer and prevent citizens from skin cancer.
Mangyan indigenous people weave sturdy nito vines into baskets that distribute heavy foraging loads evenly, preventing spinal injuries during long forest treks.
Speaking multiple Philippine languages like Tagalog and Cebuano strengthens neural pathways in the brain, helping children maintain cognitive health and improve memory.
Filipino visual artists use water-based acrylic paints instead of oil paints to avoid inhaling harmful volatile organic compounds that can damage the lungs.
